kid.question: What happens to Assyria's scattered people at the end of Nahum?

options.text: They flee into distant Egypt
They remain scattered on mountains
They gather beside the river
They surrender to neighboring kings

kid.explanation: Assyria's shepherds slumber and its people are scattered on the mountains with no one gathering them.

kid.question: Why do people clap at the news of Assyria's wound?

options.text: They have received its promised tribute
They have seen its returned captives
They have suffered its continual wickedness
They have joined its renewed alliance

kid.explanation: The closing question explains the response by asking whom Assyria's wickedness has not continually reached.

kid.question: What trouble does Habakkuk first cry out about?

options.text: Violence
Drought
Disease
Captivity

kid.explanation: Habakkuk asks how long he must cry about violence without seeing deliverance and just judgment.

kid.question: Which nation does the Lord say He is raising up?

options.text: The Egyptians
The Philistines
The Edomites
The Chaldeans

kid.explanation: The Lord announces the Chaldeans, a bitter and hasty nation taking dwellings that are not theirs.

kid.question: What picture does Habakkuk use for the conqueror taking people?

options.text: Driving sheep into an enclosed pen
Trapping birds beneath a woven basket
Catching fish with hooks and nets
Hunting deer with bows and arrows

kid.explanation: People are compared to fish taken with a hook, net, and dragnet by the conqueror.

kid.question: Where does Habakkuk say he will wait for an answer?

options.text: Inside a palace
On a watchtower
Beside a river
Within a vineyard

kid.explanation: Habakkuk sets himself on the tower to watch for what the Lord will say and how he should answer reproof.

kid.question: What does the Lord tell Habakkuk to do with the vision?

options.text: Tell it secretly to the king
Write it plainly on tablets
Sing it softly to the priests
Seal it safely in a jar

kid.explanation: The Lord commands Habakkuk to write the vision and make it plain on tables.

kid.question: Why does the Lord tell Habakkuk to wait for the vision?

options.text: It has an appointed time
It needs a second witness
It concerns a different nation
It awaits the king's approval

kid.explanation: The vision has an appointed time; though it seems to tarry, Habakkuk is told to wait because it will surely come.

kid.question: What will fill the earth like water covers the sea?

options.text: Treasure from the nations' palaces
Soldiers from the conqueror's armies
Grain from the people's harvests
Knowledge of the Lord's glory

kid.explanation: The earth will be filled with knowledge of the glory of the Lord as waters cover the sea.

kid.question: What happens to the one who has plundered many nations?

options.text: Other people will plunder him
Other people will crown him
Other people will ransom him
Other people will shelter him

kid.explanation: Because he spoiled many nations and shed blood, the remaining peoples will spoil him.

high-school.question: How does Nahum portray Assyria's leadership and people in his final lines?

options.text: Shepherds flee, nobles lead the remaining army, and people retreat behind walls
Shepherds gather flocks, nobles negotiate surrender, and people prepare a new tribute
Shepherds slumber, nobles lie in dust, and people scatter without a gatherer
Shepherds mourn, nobles choose another ruler, and people return to their fields

high-school.explanation: The terminal wound and clapping hearers are explained by the wide reach of Assyria's continual wickedness.

high-school.question: How does Habakkuk describe the effect of surrounding violence on judgment?

options.text: The law is slack and justice comes out distorted
The law is rewritten and foreign judges are appointed
The law is hidden and temple sacrifices are suspended
The law is forgotten and returning exiles reclaim their fields

high-school.explanation: Violence and strife accompany the slackened law, the wicked surrounding the righteous, and wrong judgment proceeding.

high-school.question: What role does Habakkuk acknowledge for the Chaldeans before questioning their conduct?

options.text: They are the Lord's appointed guardians of the temple and priesthood
They are the Lord's chosen messengers of warning to neighboring kingdoms
They are the Lord's chosen escorts for the return of captive families
They are the Lord's appointed instrument of judgment and correction

high-school.explanation: The Chaldeans come for violence, yet Habakkuk recognizes their appointment for judgment and questions their devouring those more righteous.

high-school.question: To whom does the conqueror attribute his power?

options.text: To his king
To his god
To his captains
To his ancestors

high-school.explanation: After scoffing at rulers and taking strongholds, the conqueror offends by attributing his power to his god.

high-school.question: Why does Habakkuk question God's silence toward the conqueror?

options.text: The invaders receive tribute but continue to besiege the capital
The conquerors capture the priests before hearing their proposed peace terms
The foreign rulers divide the land before releasing the captive families
The wicked devour people who are more righteous than themselves

high-school.explanation: Habakkuk invokes God's holiness and asks why He is silent as the wicked swallow someone more righteous.

high-school.question: Why does the conqueror sacrifice to his net and burn incense to his dragnet?

options.text: They mark the boundary assigned to his kingdom
They preserve the memory of his earlier suffering
They provide his rich portion and plentiful food
They fulfill the vow he made before leaving home

high-school.explanation: The net receives sacrifice and incense because it provides a rich portion and plentiful food, picturing trust in successful conquest.

high-school.question: How does the answer about the vision address the apparent delay?

options.text: The vision will speak at its appointed time, so Habakkuk must wait
The vision awaits approval by the king, so Habakkuk must request an audience
The vision concerns another nation, so Habakkuk must send a messenger abroad
The vision needs interpretation by priests, so Habakkuk must bring it to Jerusalem

high-school.explanation: The written vision is for an appointed time and will speak truth; the instruction is to wait, with the just living by faith.

high-school.question: What reversal is announced against the one gathering nations as possessions?

options.text: The plundered peoples will pay tribute to enlarge his treasury
The plundered peoples will rise and plunder him
The captive rulers will appoint him guardian of their temples
The captive rulers will grant him their remaining family estates

high-school.explanation: The insatiable gatherer becomes the subject of a taunt and is himself plundered because of bloodshed and violence.

high-school.question: What outcome follows the attempt to build a safe high nest through evil gain?

options.text: Building far from rivers brings drought to the fields and hunger to the household
Leaving the capital brings rebellion among the soldiers and division among the rulers
Storing tribute brings theft from the merchants and an invasion by the neighboring kings
Cutting off peoples brings shame to the house and sin against the self

high-school.explanation: Covetous gain seeks a high nest safe from harm, but cutting off peoples brings shame and even the building materials testify.

high-school.question: What contrast follows the woe against building a city with blood?

options.text: Futile human labor gives way to knowledge of the Lord's glory
Successful human labor gives way to a new royal building project
Interrupted temple service gives way to a larger annual sacrifice
Abandoned agricultural land gives way to renewed harvest tribute

high-school.explanation: Bloody construction brings labor for fire and vanity; the next verse promises earth filled with knowledge of the Lord's glory.

expert.question: What does the final question in Nahum contribute to the hearers' clapping?

options.text: It identifies their response as fulfillment of a treaty with Assyria's former allies
It interprets their response through the pervasive reach of Assyrian evil
It interprets their response through the voluntary departure of Assyrian nobles
It identifies their response as thanksgiving for Assyria's restored royal leadership

expert.explanation: The wound is unhealed and listeners clap; the rhetorical question ties their response to wickedness that has continually passed upon others.

expert.question: What progression connects Habakkuk's cry with his description of judgment?

options.text: Unanswered requests for harvest lead into a diagnosis of neglected irrigation
Rejected tribute from neighbors leads into a diagnosis of broken treaties
Rejected counsel from priests leads into a diagnosis of an interrupted sacrifice
Unanswered protest over violence leads into a diagnosis of distorted justice

expert.explanation: The complaint moves from 'how long' and violence to slackened law and judgment perverted by the wicked surrounding the righteous.

expert.question: What does Habakkuk affirm before challenging the use of the Chaldeans?

options.text: The holy, everlasting Lord has appointed them for correction
The holy, everlasting Lord has accepted their claim to permanent rule
The righteous, powerful Lord has ordered Judah to imitate their worship
The righteous, powerful Lord has assigned their captives to build His temple

expert.explanation: Habakkuk names the Lord everlasting and holy and acknowledges the conqueror's corrective role before asking about tolerated treachery.

expert.question: What comparison gives force to Habakkuk's second complaint?

options.text: The devourer is more wicked than the person he is devouring
The conqueror is more powerful than the ruler he is removing
The captive is less wealthy than the master who now owns him
The subject is less experienced than the judge who now rules him

expert.explanation: The question explicitly concerns the wicked swallowing a man more righteous than he, rather than a claim that Judah is sinless.

expert.question: What function does the fishing imagery serve across Habakkuk 1:14-17?

options.text: Human capture becomes a royal exchange that restores the captives' inheritance
Human wandering becomes a pilgrimage that renews the nation's temple service
Human capture becomes profitable conquest that feeds the conqueror's worship
Human wandering becomes a seasonal journey that supplies the fishermen's markets

expert.explanation: Rulerless fish are caught, the captor rejoices, and the successful net receives sacrifice, ending with a question about continual slaughter.

expert.question: What posture does Habakkuk adopt between complaint and divine reply?

options.text: He gathers an army and anticipates the captives' immediate return
He watches for an answer and anticipates his own reproof
He prepares a sacrifice and anticipates the priests' public approval
He appoints new judges and anticipates the king's endorsement

expert.explanation: Habakkuk takes his watch on the tower to hear what God will say and what he will answer when reproved; the Lord then responds.

expert.question: How does Habakkuk 2:3 distinguish delay from failure?

options.text: The vision may seem clear yet depends on a later prophet's correction
The vision may seem final yet applies to a different people's history
The vision may seem fulfilled yet requires another king's confirmation
The vision may seem slow yet speaks truly at its appointed time

expert.explanation: The vision is fixed to an appointed time, will not lie, and surely comes, grounding the command to wait.

expert.question: Which contrast surrounds 'the just shall live by his faith'?

options.text: The foreign ruler is not secure, and his army remains divided
The silent priest is not faithful, and his teaching remains neglected
The proud soul is not upright, and its desire remains insatiable
The captive people are not forgotten, and their inheritance remains intact

expert.explanation: The lifted-up soul is not upright; in contrast the just lives by faith, followed by further description of proud insatiability.

expert.question: What do the wall's stone and timber do in the woe against a covetous house?

options.text: The stone falls outward and the timber feeds the fire
The stone cries out and the timber gives its answer
The stone splits apart and the timber breaks the roof
The stone becomes an altar and the timber fuels sacrifice

expert.explanation: The one seeking a safe high nest through evil gain brings shame, while stone cries from the wall and timber answers.

expert.question: What reversal does the cup image announce after a neighbor is made drunk?

options.text: The offender must drink and receive shame upon his own glory
The offender must pay silver and restore the wealth of his neighbor
The offender must leave his house and surrender his inherited fields
The offender must bear a yoke and serve the captives he has taken

expert.explanation: Giving drink to expose a neighbor is answered by the Lord's cup turning to the offender and shame covering his glory.
